summary.text: A 41-year-old businessman with Familial Mediterranean Fever on long-term colchicine presented with 1 week of fever, pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness, and on arrival was hypotensive with elevated jugular venous pressure and severe respiratory distress requiring mechanical ventilator support. SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive and he was treated with tocilizumab and dexamethasone.

Initial investigations showed lymphopenia, raised CRP, fibrinogen and D-dimer, with renal markers, electrolytes and troponin T within normal limits and a normal sinus rhythm ECG. He was intubated and proned.

On day 5 of ICU admission he was found to be in complete heart block, confirmed on a 12-lead ECG. Thyroid function, cardiac biomarkers and electrolytes were unremarkable, echocardiography showed a normal ejection fraction, and the block persisted for a further three days with stable hemodynamics under conservative management and monitoring.

On day 8 of ICU admission he developed acute coronary syndrome with cardiogenic shock requiring noradrenaline and adrenaline, with ST elevation in AVR, global ST depression and a repeat echocardiogram showing global hypokinesia with an ejection fraction of 20%. He then developed ventricular tachycardia and died later that day after failed CPR.

summary.text: A 77-year-old man with no significant past medical history was brought by ambulance to the emergency department with 3 days of acute shortness of breath, severely hypoxic with SpO2 below 50% on paramedic arrival. He was intubated and proned immediately on arrival, was SARS-CoV-2 PCR positive and treated with tocilizumab and dexamethasone.

Initial workup showed lymphopenia and raised CRP, fibrinogen and D-dimer, with other laboratory results and troponin T normal, a normal sinus rhythm ECG, bilateral ground-glass opacities without pulmonary embolism on CTPA, and a normal echocardiogram.

The ICU course was complicated by shock on day 7 of admission progressing to multiorgan failure with hepatic failure and a continuous renal replacement therapy requirement. Telemetry and a 12-lead ECG showed complete heart block with occasional sinus pause, alternating with AV block despite increasing inotropic support; a temporary pacing wire was placed and permanent pacemaker implantation was scheduled.
He developed refractory hypoxic respiratory failure and was deemed unsuitable for ECMO. After family conferences the focus of care shifted to comfort measures, and he died on day 10 of admission.

summary.text: A 36-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1 with a previous Lower Segment Caesarean Section and 38 + 2 weeks pregnant, presented with 4 days of shortness of breath, fever, myalgias and diarrhea. She was febrile, tachycardic and severely hypoxic on arrival, SARS-CoV-2 PCR was positive, and she was treated with tocilizumab and dexamethasone.

Workup showed bilateral infiltrates, lymphopenia, elevated procalcitonin, normal troponin T, sinus tachycardia on the admission ECG and extensive ground-glass opacification without pulmonary embolism on CTPA. She was commenced on noninvasive ventilation, then intubated, underwent an LSCS and was admitted to ICU.

Her course was complicated by progressive hypoxemia needing prone ventilation and, on day 3, shock needing inotropic support, with echocardiogram showing global hypokinesia with ejection fraction 30% and a diagnosis of myocarditis managed with supportive care. On day 5 of ICU admission intermittent complete heart block with narrow QRS was seen and managed conservatively.

The heart block resolved gradually with improved hypoxemia, ECMO was not needed as the pAO2/FiO2 ratio improved with proning, and repeat echocardiography showed ejection fraction improved to 50%. She was discharged to another critical care facility, stable at the time of writing, with repeat echocardiography planned at outpatient cardiology follow-up.

article_limitations: Supplementary Table 1 (reference ranges) and Table 2 (event timeline for patients 1, 2 and 3) are in a DOCX supplement reviewed separately; no supplement value is copied into the main-text facts.

The discussion says initial and subsequent troponin levels were normal for all the patients; this explicitly covers every patient and contradicts the patient 1 (significantly raised troponins) and patient 2 (peak troponin T 5003 ng/L) narratives, so both sides are source_conflict/review_only; the copy to patient 3 is review_only. The sentence that echocardiography was not suggestive of underlying cardiomyopathy names no patients and stays an ambiguity.

The abstract names acute coronary syndrome for patient 1 (kept as stated) and orders CHB before multiorgan failure for patient 2 (recorded as a relation); the case text uses neither wording and does not contradict them.
Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the three ECG images are inspected in the separate visual submission.
Several inline reference markers are empty in the source text (brackets without numbers); cited literature is not attributed to any patient.

Supplement Table 2 numbers days of hospitalization; the article text uses ICU-day and admission-day counts. Supplement day labels are not converted into article times and supplement order is not used for article relations.
